competition: All-Russian Mathematical Olympiad (Final Round, Grade 9); two days, continuous numbering 1-8 as in the grade-11 row (day 1 = P1-P4, day 2 = P5-P8); translated from the official Russian papers

problems.problem: A positive integer $n$ is such that the numbers $2n+1$ and $3n+1$ are perfect squares. Can the number $5n+3$ be prime?
Segments $AB$ and $CD$ of length $1$ intersect at the point $O$, and $\angle AOC = 60^\circ$. Prove that $AC + BD \ge 1$.

A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ may be replaced by one of the trinomials $x^2f\left(\frac{1}{x}+1\right)$ or $(x-1)^2f\left(\frac{1}{x-1}\right)$. Can one obtain the trinomial $x^2+10x+9$ from the trinomial $x^2+4x+3$ by such operations?

There are ten photographs in a family album. Each of them shows three people: a man stands in the centre, his son on the left of the man, and his brother on the right. What is the smallest number of different people that can be shown on these photographs, if it is known that all ten men standing in the centre are different?
Integers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are such that $$(x-y)(y-z)(z-x) = x+y+z.$$ Prove that the number $x+y+z$ is divisible by $27$.

A convex quadrilateral is placed inside a circle; the extensions of its sides meet the circle at the points $A_1$, $A_2$, $B_1$, $B_2$, $C_1$, $C_2$, $D_1$ and $D_2$ (see the figure). Prove that if $A_1B_2 = B_1C_2 = C_1D_2 = D_1A_2$, then the quadrilateral formed by the lines $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$, $C_1C_2$, $D_1D_2$ can be inscribed in a circle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ru9_1993_p6_fig.png
What is the largest number of counters that can be placed on the squares of a chessboard so that every row, every column and every diagonal contains an even number of counters?

$n$ expressions of the form $*x^2+*x+*=0$ are written on the board ($n$ is an odd number). Two players play the following game, moving alternately. In one move a player replaces one of the asterisks by a number different from zero. After $3n$ moves one obtains $n$ quadratic equations. The first player aims to make as many of these equations as possible have no roots, while the second player tries to prevent him. What is the largest number of equations without roots that the first player can obtain regardless of the play of the second player?
Prove that if $(x+\sqrt{x^2+1})(y+\sqrt{y^2+1}) = 1$, then $x + y = 0$.

Circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ touch externally at the point $F$. A line $l$ touches $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. A line parallel to $l$ touches $S_2$ at the point $C$ and meets $S_1$ at two points. Prove that the points $A$, $F$ and $C$ lie on one line.

There are three heaps of matches on the table. The first heap contains $100$ matches, the second $200$ and the third $300$. Two players play the following game, moving alternately. In one move a player must remove one of the heaps and divide either of the remaining heaps into two non-empty parts. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his partner?

$n$ distinct blue points and $n$ distinct red points are marked on a line. Prove that the sum of the pairwise distances between points of the same colour does not exceed the sum of the pairwise distances between points of different colours.
Prove the identity $$\frac{a_1}{a_2(a_1+a_2)}+\frac{a_2}{a_3(a_2+a_3)}+\dots+\frac{a_n}{a_1(a_n+a_1)} = \frac{a_2}{a_1(a_1+a_2)}+\frac{a_3}{a_2(a_2+a_3)}+\dots+\frac{a_1}{a_n(a_n+a_1)}.$$

The positive integers from $1$ to $1000$ were written one on each card, and then some $1000$ cells of a $1\times1994$ rectangle were covered by these cards. If the cell immediately to the right of the card with the number $n$ is free, then in one move it may be covered by the card with the number $n+1$. Prove that one cannot make more than half a million such moves.

A trapezoid $ABCD$ ($AB \parallel CD$) is such that on its sides $AD$ and $BC$ there exist points $P$ and $Q$, respectively, satisfying the conditions $\angle APB = \angle CPD$, $\angle AQB = \angle CQD$. Prove that the points $P$ and $Q$ are equidistant from the intersection point of the diagonals of the trapezoid.

The plane is divided by two families of parallel lines into unit squares. The border of an $n\times n$ square consisting of squares of the partition is the union of those squares that adjoin its boundary from inside with at least one of their sides. Prove that there is exactly one way to cover a $100\times100$ square consisting of squares of the partition by non-overlapping borders of fifty squares. (The borders need not be contained in the $100\times100$ square.)
A goods train left Moscow at $x$ hours $y$ minutes and arrived in Saratov at $y$ hours $z$ minutes. The journey took $z$ hours $x$ minutes. Find all possible values of $x$.
A chord $CD$ of a circle with centre $O$ is perpendicular to its diameter $AB$, and a chord $AE$ bisects the radius $OC$. Prove that the chord $DE$ bisects the chord $BC$.
It is known that $f(x)$, $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ are quadratic trinomials. Can the equation $f(g(h(x))) = 0$ have the roots $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$ and $8$?
Can the positive integers from $1$ to $81$ be written in the cells of a $9\times9$ table so that the sum of the numbers in every $3\times3$ square is the same?

Call positive integers similar if they are written with the same set of digits (for example, for the set of digits $1, 1, 2$ the similar numbers are $112$, $121$, $211$). Prove that there exist three similar $1995$-digit numbers with no zeros in their decimal representation such that the sum of two of them equals the third.
The points $A_2$, $B_2$ and $C_2$ are the midpoints of the altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. Find the sum of the angles $B_2A_1C_2$, $C_2B_1A_2$ and $A_2C_1B_2$.

There are three heaps of stones. Sisyphus carries stones one at a time from one heap to another. For each transfer he receives from Zeus a number of coins equal to the difference between the number of stones in the heap onto which he puts the stone and the number of stones in the heap from which he takes it (the stone being moved is not counted). If this difference is negative, Sisyphus returns the corresponding sum to Zeus. (If Sisyphus cannot pay, the generous Zeus allows him to make the transfer on credit.)
At some moment it turned out that all the stones lie in the same heaps in which they lay initially. What is the largest total earning of Sisyphus at this moment?

The numbers $1$ and $-1$ are written in the cells of a $2000\times2000$ table. It is known that the sum of all numbers in the table is non-negative. Prove that one can find $1000$ rows and $1000$ columns of the table such that the sum of the numbers written in the cells at their intersections is not less than $1000$.

Which numbers are more numerous among the positive integers from $1$ to $1\,000\,000$ inclusive: those representable as the sum of a perfect square and a perfect cube, or those not representable in this form?

The centres $O_1$, $O_2$ and $O_3$ of three non-intersecting circles of the same radius are located at the vertices of a triangle. From the points $O_1$, $O_2$ and $O_3$ tangents to the given circles are drawn as shown in the figure. It is known that these tangents, intersecting, formed a convex hexagon whose sides are coloured alternately red and blue. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the red segments equals the sum of the lengths of the blue segments.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ru9_1996_p2_fig.png

Let positive integers $x$, $y$, $p$, $n$ and $k$ be such that $$x^n + y^n = p^k.$$ Prove that if the number $n$ ($n > 1$) is odd and the number $p$ is an odd prime, then $n$ is a power of the number $p$ (with a positive integer exponent).
There are $1600$ deputies in the Duma, who formed $16000$ committees of $80$ people each. Prove that there are two committees having at least four common members.
Prove that the arithmetic progression with first term $1$ and common difference $729$ contains infinitely many terms that are powers of $10$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AC = BC$) the point $O$ is the circumcentre, the point $I$ is the incentre, and the point $D$ on the side $BC$ is such that the lines $OD$ and $BI$ are perpendicular. Prove that the lines $ID$ and $AC$ are parallel.

There are two heaps of coins on the table. It is known that the total weight of the coins in the first heap equals the total weight of the coins in the second heap, and that for every positive integer $k$ not exceeding the number of coins in either heap, the total weight of the $k$ heaviest coins of the first heap is not greater than the total weight of the $k$ heaviest coins of the second heap. Prove that if every coin whose weight is not less than $x$ is replaced by a coin of weight $x$ (in both heaps), then the first heap will be not lighter than the second, whatever the positive number $x$.

Can a $5\times7$ rectangle be covered by L-trominoes (i.e. figures obtained from a $2\times2$ square by removing one cell) not extending beyond its boundary, in several layers, so that every cell of the rectangle is covered by the same number of cells belonging to the trominoes?
Let $P(x)$ be a quadratic trinomial with non-negative coefficients. Prove that for any real numbers $x$ and $y$ the inequality $$(P(xy))^2 \le P(x^2)\cdot P(y^2)$$ holds.

A convex polygon $M$ is mapped onto itself by a rotation through $90^\circ$. Prove that there exist two circles with ratio of radii equal to $\sqrt{2}$, one of which contains $M$ and the other of which is contained in $M$.

The lateral surface of a rectangular parallelepiped with base $a\times b$ and height $c$ ($a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers) is covered "along the cells", without overlaps or gaps, by rectangles with sides parallel to the edges of the parallelepiped, each consisting of an even number of unit squares. Here the rectangles may be bent over the lateral edges of the parallelepiped. Prove that if $c$ is odd, then the number of ways of covering is even.
problems.proposer: D. Karpov, S. Rukshin, D. Fon-der-Flaass

problems.problem: The re-certification of the Council of Sages takes place as follows: the king lines them up in a column one behind another and puts on each of them a cap, white or black. Every sage sees the colours of the caps of all the sages standing in front of him, but does not see the colour of his own cap or of those standing behind him. Once a minute one of the sages must call out one of the two colours (each sage calls out a colour once). After this process is over, the king executes every sage who called out a colour different from the colour of his own cap. On the eve of the re-certification all one hundred members of the Council of Sages agreed and figured out how to minimize the number of those executed. How many of them are guaranteed to avoid execution?
Do there exist real numbers $b$ and $c$ such that each of the equations $x^2+bx+c = 0$ and $2x^2+(b+1)x+c+1 = 0$ has two integer roots?

There are $33$ people in a class. Each pupil was asked how many namesakes (people with the same first name) and how many people with the same surname (including relatives) he has in the class. It turned out that among the numbers given were all integers from $0$ to $10$ inclusive. Prove that there are two pupils in the class with the same first name and surname.

The circle inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ touches its sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ at the points $M$, $N$ and $K$ respectively. The line through the vertex $A$ parallel to $NK$ meets the line $MN$ at the point $D$. The line through $A$ parallel to $MN$ meets the line $NK$ at the point $E$. Prove that the line $DE$ contains a midline of the triangle $ABC$.

The numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, 100$ are placed in the cells of a $10\times10$ table so that the sum of any two neighbouring numbers does not exceed $S$. Find the smallest possible value of $S$. (Numbers are called neighbouring if they stand in cells having a common side.)

The angle formed by the rays $y = x$ and $y = 2x$ for $x \ge 0$ cuts off two arcs on the parabola $y = x^2+px+q$. These arcs are projected onto the axis $Ox$. Prove that the projection of the left arc is shorter by $1$ than the projection of the right arc.
A convex polygon is divided into parallelograms. A vertex of the polygon belonging to only one parallelogram is called good. Prove that there are at least three good vertices.
Denote by $S(x)$ the sum of the digits of the number $x$. Do there exist three positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $S(a+b) < 5$, $S(a+c) < 5$ and $S(b+c) < 5$, but $S(a+b+c) > 50$?

A labyrinth is an $8\times8$ chessboard on which walls are placed between some squares. On the command RIGHT a rook moves one square to the right or, if there is the edge of the board or a wall on the right, stays where it is; the commands LEFT, UP and DOWN are executed similarly. A programmer writes a program, a finite sequence of these commands, and gives it to a user, after which the user chooses a labyrinth and places a rook in it on any square. Is it true that the programmer can write a program such that the rook visits all accessible squares of the labyrinth for every choice of the user?

There are $5$ clocks with hands on a table. It is allowed to move any number of them forward. For each clock, the time by which it is moved forward is called its shifting time. All clocks are required to be set so that they show the same time. What is the smallest total shifting time with which this can be guaranteed?

In a triangle $ABC$ ($AB > BC$) the median $BM$ and the bisector $BL$ are drawn. The line through the point $M$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BL$ at the point $D$, and the line through $L$ parallel to $BC$ meets $BM$ at the point $E$. Prove that the lines $ED$ and $BL$ are perpendicular.

A jeweller made an open chain of $N > 3$ numbered links. A capricious customer demanded that the order of the links in the chain be changed. Out of spite she ordered an open chain such that the jeweller had to open as many links as possible. How many links will have to be opened?

Two distinct positive integers $a$ and $b$ are written on the board. The smaller of them is erased and the number $\frac{ab}{|a-b|}$ is written instead (which may already be a non-integer). The same operation is performed with the resulting pair of numbers, and so on. Prove that at some moment two equal positive integers will be on the board.
In the number $A$ the digits are in increasing order (from left to right). What is the sum of the digits of the number $9\cdot A$?

There are several cities in a country; some pairs of cities are connected by non-stop flights of one of $N$ airlines, and from every city there is exactly one flight of each of the airlines. It is known that from any city one can fly to any other (possibly with changes). Because of a financial crisis $N-1$ flights were closed, but no airline closed more than one flight. Prove that it is still possible to fly from any city to any other.

A triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $S$. Let $A_0$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of the circle $S$ not containing $A$, and $C_0$ the midpoint of the arc $AB$ not containing $C$. The circle $S_1$ with centre $A_0$ touches $BC$, and the circle $S_2$ with centre $C_0$ touches $AB$. Prove that the incentre $I$ of the triangle $ABC$ lies on one of the common external tangents to the circles $S_1$ and $S_2$.

The numbers from $1$ to $1\,000\,000$ are coloured in two colours, black and white. In one move one may choose any number from $1$ to $1\,000\,000$ and recolour it and all numbers not coprime to it into the opposite colour. Initially all numbers were black. Can one achieve, after several moves, that all numbers become white?

An equilateral triangle is divided into equilateral triangles with side $1$ by lines parallel to its sides that divide each side into $n$ parts (in the figure $n = 5$).
What is the largest number of segments of length $1$ with endpoints at vertices of these triangles that can be marked so that there is no triangle all of whose sides consist of marked segments?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ru9_1999_p5_fig.png
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ the inequality $$\sum_{k=1}^{n^2}\{\sqrt{k}\}\le\frac{n^2-1}{2}$$ holds. ($\{k\}$ denotes the fractional part of the number $k$.)

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the side $BC$ at the point $D$. A circle passing through the vertices $B$ and $C$ meets the side $AB$ at the point $E$ and meets the first circle again at the point $F$. It turned out that the points $A$, $E$, $D$, $C$ lie on a circle with centre $O$. Prove that the angle $BFO$ is a right angle.

In a microchip there are $2000$ contacts, and initially every two contacts are connected by a separate wire. The hooligans Vasya and Petya cut the wires in turn, Vasya (who starts) cutting one wire per move, and Petya cutting either one or three wires. The hooligan who cuts the last wire from some contact loses. Who wins with correct play?

Distinct numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that the equations $x^2+ax+1 = 0$ and $x^2+bx+c = 0$ have a common real root. Moreover, the equations $x^2+x+a = 0$ and $x^2+cx+b = 0$ have a common real root. Find the sum $a+b+c$.

Tanya has thought of a positive integer $X \le 100$, and Sasha is trying to guess it. He chooses a pair of positive integers $M$ and $N$ less than $100$ and asks: "What is the greatest common divisor of $X+M$ and $N$?" Prove that Sasha can guess Tanya's number by asking $7$ such questions.

Let $O$ be the centre of the circumcircle $\omega$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. A circle $\omega_1$ with centre $K$ passes through the points $A$, $O$, $C$ and meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at the points $M$ and $N$. It is known that the points $L$ and $K$ are symmetric with respect to the line $MN$. Prove that $BL \perp AC$.
There are several cities in a country; some pairs of cities are connected by roads. At least $3$ roads leave every city. Prove that there exists a cyclic route whose length is not divisible by $3$.

The numbers $a_1 = 1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ are written on the board one after another according to the following rules: $a_{n+1} = a_n-2$ if the number $a_n-2$ is a positive integer that has not yet been written on the board; otherwise $a_{n+1} = a_n+3$. Prove that all squares of positive integers will appear in this sequence when $3$ is added to the preceding number.

Black and white counters stand on some cells of a $2n\times2n$ board. First all black counters that stand in the same column as some white counter are removed from the board, and then all white counters that stand in the same row as some of the remaining black ones. Prove that either black or white counters remain on the board in number not exceeding $n^2$.

A point $E$ is marked on the median $CD$ of a triangle $ABC$. The circle $S_1$ passing through $E$ and tangent to the line $AB$ at the point $A$ meets the side $AC$ at the point $M$. The circle $S_2$ passing through $E$ and tangent to the line $AB$ at the point $B$ meets the side $BC$ at the point $N$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $CMN$ is tangent to $S_1$ and $S_2$.

$100$ positive integers, coprime as a whole, are placed around a circle. It is allowed to add to any number the greatest common divisor of its neighbours. Prove that by such operations one can make all the numbers pairwise coprime.

The numbers from $1$ to $999\,999$ are divided into two groups: the first group contains every number for which the square nearest to it is the square of an odd number, the second the numbers for which the nearest squares are squares of even numbers. In which group is the sum of the numbers larger?

Two polynomials $P(x) = x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ and $Q(x) = x^2+px+q$ take negative values on some interval $I$ of length greater than $2$, and outside $I$ they are non-negative. Prove that there exists a point $x_0$ such that $P(x_0) < Q(x_0)$.

Inside a parallelogram $ABCD$ with obtuse angle $A$ a point $K$ is chosen such that the midpoint of the segment $AD$ is equidistant from the points $K$ and $C$, and the midpoint of the segment $CD$ is equidistant from the points $K$ and $A$. The point $N$ is the midpoint of the segment $BK$. Prove that the angles $NAK$ and $NCK$ are equal.

A convex $2000$-gon is given, no three diagonals of which pass through one point. Each of its diagonals is coloured in one of $999$ colours. Prove that there exists a triangle all of whose sides lie entirely on diagonals of one colour. (The vertices of the triangle need not be vertices of the original polygon.)

Yura laid out in a row $2001$ coins of denominations $1$, $2$ and $3$ kopecks. It turned out that between any two one-kopeck coins there is at least one coin, between any two two-kopeck coins there are at least two coins, and between any two three-kopeck coins there are at least three coins. How many three-kopeck coins could Yura have?
In a company of $2n+1$ people, for any $n$ people there is a person different from them who is acquainted with each of them. Prove that there is a person in this company who knows everybody.

A point $N$ is taken on the largest side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ such that the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $AN$ and $NC$ meet the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at the points $K$ and $M$ respectively. Prove that the circumcentre $O$ of the triangle $ABC$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $KBM$.
Find all odd positive integers $n$ ($n > 1$) such that for any coprime divisors $a$ and $b$ of the number $n$ the number $a+b-1$ is also a divisor of $n$.

Can the positive integers from $1$ to $2002^2$ be placed in the cells of a $2002\times2002$ table so that for every cell of this table one can choose, from the row or from the column containing this cell, a triple of numbers one of which equals the product of the other two?

On one side of an angle with vertex $O$ a point $A$ is taken, and on the other side points $B$ and $C$ such that $B$ lies between $O$ and $C$. The circle with centre $O_1$ inscribed in the triangle $OAB$ and the circle with centre $O_2$ touching the side $AC$ and the extensions of the sides $OA$, $OC$ of the triangle $OAC$ are drawn. Prove that if $O_1A = O_2A$, then the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

$6$ red, $6$ blue and $6$ green points are marked in the plane, no three of the marked points lying on one line. Prove that the sum of the areas of the triangles with vertices of the same colour is at most a quarter of the sum of the areas of all triangles with marked vertices.

Hydras consist of heads and necks (each neck joins exactly two heads). With one blow of a sword one can cut off all the necks leaving some head $A$ of the hydra. But then from the head $A$ there instantly grows one neck to every head with which $A$ was not joined. Heracles defeats the hydra if he manages to cut it into two parts not joined by necks. Find the smallest $N$ for which Heracles can defeat any hydra with $100$ necks by striking at most $N$ blows.

There are $8$ rooks on a chessboard, no two attacking each other. Prove that among the pairwise distances between them there are two equal ones. (The distance between rooks is the distance between the centres of the squares on which they stand.)

There are one red and $k$ ($k > 1$) blue cells, and also a deck of $2n$ cards numbered $1$ to $2n$. Initially the whole deck lies, in arbitrary order, in the red cell. From any cell one may take the top card and put it either into an empty cell or on top of a card whose number is greater by one. For what largest $n$ can the whole deck be moved into one of the blue cells by such operations?

Let $O$ be the circumcentre of a triangle $ABC$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ points $M$ and $N$ respectively are chosen so that $2\angle MON = \angle AOC$. Prove that the perimeter of the triangle $MBN$ is not less than the side $AC$.
$2^{2n-1}+1$ odd numbers are chosen from the interval $(2^{2n}, 2^{3n})$. Prove that among the chosen numbers there are two such that the square of each of them is not divisible by the other.

A set of numbers $M$ containing $2003$ distinct numbers is such that for any two distinct elements $a, b$ of $M$ the number $a^2+b\sqrt{2}$ is rational. Prove that for every $a$ in $M$ the number $a\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

Circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ with centres $O_1$ and $O_2$ respectively meet at the points $A$ and $B$. The tangents to $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the point $A$ meet the segments $BO_2$ and $BO_1$ at the points $K$ and $L$ respectively. Prove that $KL \parallel O_1O_2$.

On a line there are $2k-1$ white and $2k-1$ black segments. It is known that every white segment intersects at least $k$ black ones, and every black segment at least $k$ white ones. Prove that there exist a black segment intersecting all the white ones and a white segment intersecting all the black ones.

The sequence $\{a_n\}$ is constructed as follows: $a_1 = p$ is a prime number having exactly $300$ non-zero digits, and $a_{n+1}$ is the period of the decimal fraction $1/a_n$ multiplied by $2$. Find the number $a_{2003}$.

There are $N$ cities in a country. Between any two of them there is either a motor road or a railway. A tourist wants to travel round the country, visiting each city exactly once, and return to the city where he started his journey. Prove that the tourist can choose the city from which he starts the journey and a route such that he will have to change the kind of transport at most once.
Let $a, b, c$ be positive numbers whose sum equals $1$. Prove the inequality $$\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}\ge\frac{2}{1+a}+\frac{2}{1+b}+\frac{2}{1+c}.$$

Can positive integers be placed in the cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper so that for any positive integers $m, n > 100$ the sum of the numbers in every $m\times n$ rectangle of cells is divisible by $m+n$?

On the sides $AP$ and $PD$ of an acute triangle $APD$ points $B$ and $C$ respectively are chosen. The diagonals of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at the point $Q$. The points $H_1$ and $H_2$ are the orthocentres of the triangles $APD$ and $BPC$ respectively. Prove that if the line $H_1H_2$ passes through the point $X$ of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $ABQ$ and $CDQ$, then it also passes through the point $Y$ of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $BQC$ and $AQD$. ($X \ne Q$, $Y \ne Q$.)
Every lattice point of the plane is coloured in one of three colours, and all three colours occur. Prove that there exists a right triangle with vertices of three different colours.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is circumscribed about a circle. The bisectors of the exterior angles $A$ and $B$ meet at the point $K$, those of the exterior angles $B$ and $C$ at the point $L$, those of the exterior angles $C$ and $D$ at the point $M$, and those of the exterior angles $D$ and $A$ at the point $N$. Let $K_1$, $L_1$, $M_1$, $N_1$ be the orthocentres of the triangles $ABK$, $BCL$, $CDM$, $DAN$ respectively. Prove that the quadrilateral $K_1L_1M_1N_1$ is a parallelogram.

There are $2004$ boxes on a table, each containing one ball. It is known that some of the balls are white, and their number is even. It is allowed to point at any two boxes and ask whether there is at least one white ball in them. What is the smallest number of questions with which one can determine with certainty some two boxes containing white balls?

A positive integer $n > 3$ and positive numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ whose product equals $1$ are given. Prove the inequality $$\frac{1}{1+x_1+x_1x_2}+\frac{1}{1+x_2+x_2x_3}+\dots+\frac{1}{1+x_n+x_nx_1} > 1.$$
Do there exist pairwise distinct positive integers $m$, $n$, $p$, $q$ such that $m+n = p+q$ and $\sqrt{m}+\sqrt[3]{n} = \sqrt{p}+\sqrt[3]{q} > 2004$?

There are $2004$ telephones in the president's office, any two of which are connected by a wire of one of four colours. It is known that wires of all four colours occur. Is it always possible to choose several telephones so that among the wires connecting them there are wires of exactly three colours?

The positive integers from $1$ to $100$ are arranged around a circle in such an order that every number is either greater than both its neighbours or smaller than both its neighbours. A pair of neighbouring numbers is called good if, after this pair is thrown out, the property described above is preserved. What is the minimal possible number of good pairs?

Let $O$ be the circumcentre of an acute triangle $ABC$, $T$ the circumcentre of the triangle $AOC$, and $M$ the midpoint of $AC$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ points $D$ and $E$ respectively are chosen such that $\angle BDM = \angle BEM = \angle ABC$. Prove that $BT \perp DE$.

A parallelogram $ABCD$ ($AB < BC$) is given. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $APQ$, for all possible points $P$ and $Q$ chosen on the sides $BC$ and $CD$ respectively so that $CP = CQ$, have a common point different from $A$.

Lyosha placed the positive integers from $1$ to $22^2$ in the cells of a $22\times22$ table. Is it true that Oleg can choose two cells adjacent by a side or by a vertex such that the sum of the numbers standing in these cells is divisible by $4$?

The sum of the numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3$, each of which is greater than one, equals $S$, and $\frac{a_i^2}{a_i-1} > S$ for every $i = 1, 2, 3$. Prove that $$\frac{1}{a_1+a_2}+\frac{1}{a_2+a_3}+\frac{1}{a_3+a_1} > 1.$$

There are $365$ cards on the table, on the backs of which distinct numbers are written. For one rouble Vasya may choose three cards and ask Petya to put them from left to right so that the numbers on the cards are in increasing order. Can Vasya, having spent $2000$ roubles, be sure to lay out all $365$ cards on the table from left to right so that the numbers on them are in increasing order?
Ten pairwise distinct non-zero numbers are such that for any two of them either the sum of these numbers or their product is a rational number. Prove that the squares of all the numbers are rational.

In how many ways can the numbers $2^0, 2^1, 2^2, \dots, 2^{2005}$ be divided into two non-empty sets $A$ and $B$ so that the equation $x^2-S(A)x+S(B) = 0$, where $S(M)$ is the sum of the numbers of the set $M$, has an integer root?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA'$ and $BB'$ are drawn. A point $D$ is chosen on the arc $ACB$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. Let the lines $AA'$ and $BD$ meet at the point $P$, and the lines $BB'$ and $AD$ at the point $Q$. Prove that the line $A'B'$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $PQ$.

$100$ representatives of $50$ countries, two from each country, sit at a round table. Prove that they can be divided into two groups so that each group contains one representative of each country and every person is in the same group as at most one of his neighbours.

A $15\times15$ board is given. Some pairs of centres of cells adjacent by a side were joined by segments so that a closed non-self-intersecting polygonal line was obtained which is symmetric with respect to one of the diagonals of the board. Prove that the length of the polygonal line is not greater than $200$.
Prove that there exist $4$ integers $a, b, c, d$, each greater than $1\,000\,000$ in absolute value, such that $$\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d} = \frac{1}{abcd}.$$

Petya colours $2006$ points located on a circle in $17$ colours. Then Kolya draws chords with endpoints at the marked points so that the endpoints of every chord have the same colour and the chords have no common points (including common endpoints). Kolya wants to draw as many chords as possible, while Petya tries to prevent him. What is the largest number of chords that Kolya can certainly draw?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. A circle $\omega$ touches the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at the point $A$, meets the side $AB$ at the point $K$, and also meets the side $BC$. The tangent $CL$ to the circle $\omega$ is such that the segment $KL$ meets the side $BC$ at the point $T$. Prove that the segment $BT$ is equal in length to the tangent from the point $B$ to $\omega$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{10}$ be positive integers, $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_{10}$. Let $b_k$ be the largest divisor of $a_k$ such that $b_k < a_k$. It turned out that $b_1 > b_2 > \dots > b_{10}$. Prove that $a_{10} > 500$.

On the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ of a triangle $ABC$ points $P$, $Q$, $R$ respectively are chosen such that $AP = CQ$ and the quadrilateral $RPBQ$ is cyclic. The tangents to the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at the points $A$ and $C$ meet the lines $RP$ and $RQ$ at the points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Prove that $RX = RY$.

A $100\times100$ square of cells is cut into dominoes: $1\times2$ rectangles. Two players play a game. In each move a player glues together two cells adjacent by a side between which a cut was made. A player loses if after his move the figure becomes connected, i.e. the whole square can be lifted from the table by holding it by one cell. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?
A quadratic trinomial $f(x) = x^2+ax+b$ is given. The equation $f(f(x)) = 0$ has four distinct real roots, the sum of two of which equals $-1$. Prove that $b \le -\frac{1}{4}$.

Monic quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are such that the equations $f(g(x)) = 0$ and $g(f(x)) = 0$ have no real roots. Prove that at least one of the equations $f(f(x)) = 0$ and $g(g(x)) = 0$ also has no real roots.

$100$ fractions were written on the board, whose numerators are all the numbers from $1$ to $100$, each once, and whose denominators are all the numbers from $1$ to $100$, each once. It turned out that the sum of these fractions is an irreducible fraction with denominator $2$. Prove that one can interchange the numerators of two fractions so that the sum becomes an irreducible fraction with odd denominator.

Two players take turns drawing diagonals in a regular $(2n+1)$-gon ($n > 1$). A diagonal may be drawn if it intersects (at interior points) an even number of previously drawn diagonals (and has not been drawn before). The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins with correct play?

In a triangle $ABC$ the bisector $BB_1$ is drawn. The perpendicular from $B_1$ to $BC$ meets the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at the point $K$. The perpendicular from $B$ to $AK$ meets $AC$ at the point $L$. Prove that the points $K$, $L$ and the midpoint of the arc $AC$ (not containing the point $B$) lie on one line.
Two distinct numbers are written at each vertex of a convex $100$-gon. Prove that one can cross out one number at each vertex so that the remaining numbers at any two adjacent vertices are different.

An acute triangle $ABC$ is given. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $BC$ respectively, and the point $H$ is the foot of the altitude dropped from the vertex $B$. The circumcircles of the triangles $AHN$ and $CHM$ meet at the point $P$ ($P \ne H$). Prove that the line $PH$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $MN$.

The numbers from $1$ to $100$ are placed in a $10\times10$ table: in the first row from $1$ to $10$ from left to right, in the second from $11$ to $20$ from left to right, and so on. Andrei is going to cut the table into $1\times2$ rectangles, compute the product of the numbers in each rectangle and add up the resulting $50$ numbers. He wants to obtain as small a sum as possible. How should he cut the square?

Dima computed the factorials of all positive integers from $80$ to $99$, found their reciprocals, and printed the resulting decimal fractions on $20$ infinite tapes (for example, the last tape had the number $\frac{1}{99!} = 0.\underbrace{00\ldots00}_{155\text{ zeros}}10715\ldots$ printed on it). Sasha wants to cut out of one tape a piece on which $N$ consecutive digits are written and there is no decimal point. For what largest $N$ can he do this so that Dima cannot determine from this piece which tape Sasha has spoiled?
Do there exist $14$ positive integers such that, when each of them is increased by $1$, the product of all the numbers increases exactly $2008$ times?
Numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that the equation $x^3+ax^2+bx+c = 0$ has three real roots. Prove that if $-2 \le a+b+c \le 0$, then at least one of these roots belongs to the segment $[0,2]$.

In a scalene triangle $ABC$ the points $H$ and $M$ are the intersection points of the altitudes and of the medians respectively. Through the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ lines perpendicular to the lines $AM$, $BM$, $CM$ respectively are drawn. Prove that the centroid of the triangle formed by these lines lies on the line $MH$.

Several research workers work at NIICHAVO. During an $8$-hour working day the workers went to the canteen, possibly several times. It is known that for every two workers the total time during which exactly one of them was in the canteen was at least $x$ hours ($x > 4$). What is the largest number of research workers who could have worked at NIICHAVO on that day (depending on $x$)?

Call the distance between two cells of an infinite chessboard the minimal number of moves of a king on a path between these cells. Three cells are marked on the board, the pairwise distances between which are equal to $100$. How many cells are there whose distances to all three marked cells are equal to $50$?

The incircle touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ at the points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. The point $K$ is the midpoint of the arc $AB$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. It turned out that the line $XY$ bisects the segment $AK$. What can the angle $BAC$ be equal to?

A positive integer is written on the board. If the number $x$ is written on the board, then one may additionally write on it the number $2x+1$ or $\frac{x}{x+2}$. At some moment it turned out that the number $2008$ is on the board. Prove that it was there from the very beginning.

We have $3^{2k}$ outwardly indistinguishable coins, one of which is counterfeit: it weighs slightly less than a genuine one. Moreover, we have three two-pan balances. It is known that two of the balances are correct and one is broken (the outcome it shows is in no way related to the weight of the coins put on it, i.e. it may be correct or distorted in either direction, and distorted differently in different weighings). It is not known which balances are correct and which is broken. How can one determine the counterfeit coin in $3k+1$ weighings?
The denominators of two irreducible fractions are $600$ and $700$. Find the smallest possible value of the denominator of their sum (in irreducible form).

In a triangle $ABC$ the bisector $BD$ is drawn (the point $D$ lies on the segment $AC$). The line $BD$ meets the circle $\Omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ at the points $B$ and $E$. The circle $\omega$ constructed on the segment $DE$ as diameter meets the circle $\Omega$ at the points $E$ and $F$. Prove that the line symmetric to the line $BF$ with respect to the line $BD$ contains a median of the triangle $ABC$.

A positive integer $n > 1$ is given. A number $a > n^2$ is such that among the numbers $a+1, a+2, \dots, a+n$ there are multiples of each of the numbers $n^2+1, n^2+2, \dots, n^2+n$. Prove that $a > n^4-n^3$.

$100$ thimbles stand in a circle. A coin is hidden under one of them. In one move one may turn over four thimbles and check whether the coin lies under one of them. After that they are returned to their original position, and the coin moves under one of the thimbles adjacent to it. What is the smallest number of moves needed to be sure to find the coin?
Numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) = abc, \qquad (a^3+b^3)(b^3+c^3)(c^3+a^3) = a^3b^3c^3.$$ Prove that $abc = 0$.

Can the positive integers be coloured in $2009$ colours so that each colour occurs infinitely many times and there is no triple of numbers coloured in three different colours such that the product of two of them equals the third?

The eight cells of one diagonal of a chessboard are called the fence. A rook moves over the board, never stepping on the same cell twice and never stepping on the cells of the fence (intermediate cells are not considered visited). What is the largest number of jumps over the fence that the rook can make?

Triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ have equal areas. Is it always possible to construct with compass and straightedge a triangle $A_2B_2C_2$ congruent to the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ such that the lines $AA_2$, $BB_2$ and $CC_2$ are parallel?

There are $24$ pencils of four colours, $6$ pencils of each colour. They were distributed among $6$ children so that each received $4$ pencils. What is the smallest number of children that one can always choose so that they are guaranteed to have pencils of all colours, regardless of the distribution of the pencils?

$100$ pairwise distinct numbers are placed around a circle. Prove that one can choose $4$ consecutive numbers such that the sum of the two outer numbers of this quadruple is strictly greater than the sum of the two middle ones.

The lines tangent to a circle $\omega$ at the points $A$ and $B$ meet at the point $O$. The point $I$ is the centre of $\omega$. On the smaller arc $AB$ of the circle $\omega$ a point $C$ is chosen, different from the midpoint of the arc. The lines $AC$ and $OB$ meet at the point $D$, and the lines $BC$ and $OA$ at the point $E$. Prove that the circumcentres of the triangles $ACE$, $BCD$ and $OCI$ lie on one line.

There are $100$ apples of total weight $10$ kg in a canteen, each weighing at least $25$ g. The canteen worker has to cut them into pieces and give them to $100$ children, $100$ g to each. Prove that she can do this so that every piece of apple weighs at least $25$ g.
Distinct real numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that the equation $$(x^2+20ax+10b)(x^2+20bx+10a) = 0$$ has no roots. Prove that the number $20(b-a)$ is not an integer.

Each of $1000$ gnomes has a cap that is blue on the outside and red on the inside (or vice versa). If a gnome wears a red cap, he can only lie, and if a blue one, he can only tell the truth. During one day every gnome said to every other gnome: "You are wearing a red cap!" (during the day some gnomes turned their caps inside out). Find the smallest possible number of turnings inside out.
Call a positive integer $n$ unlucky if it cannot be represented in the form $n = \dfrac{x^2-1}{y^2-1}$ with positive integers $x, y > 1$. Is the number of unlucky numbers finite or infinite?
In an acute triangle $ABC$ the median $AM$ is longer than the side $AB$. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ can be cut into three parts from which a rhombus can be assembled.
A quadratic trinomial $P(x)$ with leading coefficient $1$ is such that the polynomials $P(x)$ and $P(P(P(x)))$ have a common root. Prove that $P(0)\cdot P(1) = 0$.

An acute triangle $ABC$ is given. A circle passing through the vertex $B$ and the centre $O$ of its circumcircle meets the sides $BC$ and $BA$ a second time at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that the orthocentre of the triangle $POQ$ lies on the line $AC$.

A convex $2011$-gon is drawn on the board. Petya successively draws diagonals in it so that each newly drawn diagonal intersects at interior points at most one of the previously drawn diagonals. What is the largest number of diagonals Petya can draw?
Do there exist three positive integers, coprime as a whole, such that the square of each of them is divisible by the sum of the other two?

For some $2011$ positive integers all their $2011\cdot2010/2$ pairwise sums were written on the board. Could it happen that exactly one third of the written sums is divisible by $3$, and another exactly one third of them leave remainder $1$ upon division by $3$?

Petya and Kolya each have two numbers written in their notebooks; initially these are the numbers $1$ and $2$ for Petya and $3$ and $4$ for Kolya. Once a minute Petya forms a quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ whose roots are the two numbers written in his notebook, and Kolya forms a quadratic trinomial $g(x)$ whose roots are the two numbers written in his notebook. If the equation $f(x) = g(x)$ has two distinct roots, then one of the boys replaces his pair of numbers by these roots; otherwise nothing happens. What could the second number in Petya's notebook be at the moment when the first one became equal to $5$?

Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle. On its side $AC$ a point $T$ is chosen, and on the arcs $AB$ and $BC$ of its circumcircle points $M$ and $N$ respectively are chosen so that $MT \parallel BC$ and $NT \parallel AB$. The segments $AN$ and $MT$ meet at the point $X$, and the segments $CM$ and $NT$ at the point $Y$. Prove that the perimeters of the polygons $AXYC$ and $XMBNY$ are equal.

Some cells of a $100\times100$ board contain one counter each. Call a cell beautiful if the cells adjacent to it by a side contain an even number of counters. Can exactly one cell of the board be beautiful?

Let $a_1, \dots, a_{11}$ be distinct positive integers not less than $2$ whose sum equals $407$. Could it happen that the sum of the remainders of the division of some positive integer $n$ by the $22$ numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{11}, 4a_1, 4a_2, \dots, 4a_{11}$ equals $2012$?

$2012$ points dividing a circle into equal arcs are marked on it. Of these, $k$ points were chosen, and a convex $k$-gon with vertices at the chosen points was constructed. For what largest $k$ could it happen that this polygon has no parallel sides?

A parallelogram $ABCD$ with obtuse angle $A$ is given. The point $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the point $A$ to $BC$. The extension of the median of the triangle $ABC$ drawn from the vertex $C$ meets its circumcircle at the point $K$. Prove that the points $K$, $H$, $C$ and $D$ lie on one circle.

Positive real numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $k$ are such that $a_1+\dots+a_n = 3k$, $a_1^2+\dots+a_n^2 = 3k^2$ and $a_1^3+\dots+a_n^3 > 3k^3+k$. Prove that some two of the numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ differ by more than $1$.

$101$ sages stand in a circle. Each of them believes either that the Earth revolves around Jupiter or that Jupiter revolves around the Earth. Once a minute all the sages simultaneously announce their opinions. Immediately after this, every sage both of whose neighbours think differently from him changes his opinion, while the others do not change theirs. Prove that after some time the opinions will stop changing.

Points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively. It turned out that $AB_1-AC_1 = CA_1-CB_1 = BC_1-BA_1$. Let $I_A$, $I_B$ and $I_C$ be the incentres of the triangles $AB_1C_1$, $A_1BC_1$ and $A_1B_1C$ respectively. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $I_AI_BI_C$ coincides with the incentre of the triangle $ABC$.

Initially $10$ consecutive positive integers are written on the board. In one operation one may choose any two numbers on the board (denote them by $a$ and $b$) and replace them by the numbers $a^2-2011b^2$ and $ab$. After several such operations none of the original numbers remained on the board. Could there again be $10$ consecutive positive integers on the board?

In a certain city the network of bus routes is arranged so that any two routes have exactly one common stop, and every route has at least $4$ stops. Prove that all stops can be distributed between two companies so that every route has stops of both companies.
Distinct real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given. Prove that at least two of the equations $(x-a)(x-b) = x-c$, $(x-b)(x-c) = x-a$, $(x-c)(x-a) = x-b$ have a solution.

An acute triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. The tangents to $\Omega$ at the points $B$ and $C$ meet at the point $P$. The points $D$ and $E$ are the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from the point $P$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that the orthocentre of the triangle $ADE$ is the midpoint of the segment $BC$.

$100$ pairwise distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{100}$ were written on the board. Then under each number $a_i$ the number $b_i$ was written, obtained by adding to $a_i$ the greatest common divisor of the other $99$ original numbers. What is the smallest number of pairwise distinct numbers that can be among $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{100}$?

$n$ lines are drawn in the plane, no two of which are parallel and no three of which pass through one point. Prove that there exists an $n$-link non-self-intersecting polygonal line $A_0A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ such that each of the $n$ lines contains exactly one link of this polygonal line.

$2n$ real numbers whose sum is positive are placed around a circle. For each of them consider both groups of $n$ consecutive numbers in which this number is an end one. Prove that there is a number for which the sum of the numbers in each of the two such groups is positive.

Petya and Vasya came up with ten quadratic trinomials. Then Vasya named consecutive positive integers one after another (starting from some number), and Petya substituted each named number into one of the trinomials of his choice and wrote the values obtained on the board from left to right. It turned out that the numbers written on the board form an arithmetic progression (in exactly this order). What is the largest number of numbers Vasya could have named?

Squares $CAKL$ and $CBMN$ are constructed outwards on the sides of an acute triangle $ABC$. The line $CN$ meets the segment $AK$ at the point $X$, and the line $CL$ meets the segment $BM$ at the point $Y$. The point $P$ lying inside the triangle $ABC$ is the intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $KXN$ and $LYM$. The point $S$ is the midpoint of the segment $AB$. Prove that $\angle ACS = \angle BCP$.

From a $55\times55$ square of cells, $400$ L-shaped three-cell pieces (rotated in any way) and another $500$ single cells were cut out along the cell boundaries. Prove that some two of the cut-out figures have a common segment of their boundary.

$99$ positive integers are arranged around a circle. It is known that any two neighbouring numbers differ either by $1$, or by $2$, or by a factor of two. Prove that at least one of these numbers is divisible by $3$.

Seryozha chose two distinct positive integers $a$ and $b$. He wrote four numbers in his notebook: $a$, $a+2$, $b$ and $b+2$. Then he wrote on the board all six pairwise products of the numbers from the notebook. What is the largest number of perfect squares that can be among the numbers on the board?

Several diagonals are drawn in a convex $n$-gon. A drawn diagonal is called good if it intersects (at interior points) exactly one of the other drawn diagonals. Find the largest possible number of good diagonals.

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ in which $AB > BC$. The circle $\Omega$ is circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$. The tangents to $\Omega$ at the points $A$ and $C$ meet at the point $P$. The segments $BP$ and $AC$ meet at the point $S$. Let $AD$ be an altitude of the triangle $ABP$. The circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $CSD$ meets the circle $\Omega$ at the point $K \ne C$. Prove that $\angle CKM = 90^\circ$.
To a positive integer $N$ its largest divisor smaller than $N$ was added, and a power of ten was obtained. Find all such $N$.

A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. A circle $\omega$ passes through the points $C$, $D$ and meets the segments $CA$, $CB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ respectively. The points $A_2$ and $B_2$ are symmetric to the points $A_1$ and $B_1$ with respect to the midpoints of the segments $CA$ and $CB$ respectively. Prove that the points $A$, $B$, $A_2$ and $B_2$ lie on one circle.

In the republic of mathematicians a number $\alpha > 2$ was chosen, and coins of denominations $1$ rouble and $\alpha^k$ roubles for every positive integer $k$ were issued. Here $\alpha$ was chosen so that the denominations of all coins except the smallest one are irrational. Could it happen that every sum of a positive integer number of roubles can be made up from these coins using coins of each denomination at most $6$ times?

There are $n$ cities in a state, and between every two of them an express train runs (in both directions). For each express train the ticket prices "there" and "back" are equal, and for any different express trains these prices are different. Prove that a traveller can choose a starting city, leave it and travel successively on $n-1$ express trains, paying for each next ride less than for the previous one. (The traveller may visit the same city several times.)

Numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that each of the two quadratic trinomials $x^2+ax+b$ and $x^2+bx+a$ has two distinct roots, and the product of these trinomials has exactly three distinct roots. Find all possible values of the sum of these three roots.

A parallelogram $ABCD$ is such that $\angle B < 90^\circ$ and $AB < BC$. Points $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ so that the tangents to $\omega$ at these points pass through $D$. It turned out that $\angle EDA = \angle FDC$. Find the angle $ABC$.
Positive integers $a$, $x$ and $y$, greater than $100$, are such that $y^2-1 = a^2(x^2-1)$. What is the smallest value that the fraction $a/x$ can take?

$110$ teams took part in a volleyball tournament, each playing every other exactly once (there are no draws in volleyball). It turned out that in any group of $55$ teams there is one that lost to at most four of the other $54$ teams of this group. Prove that in the whole tournament there is a team that lost to at most four of the other $109$ teams.

$100$ integers are written around a circle. Each of the numbers is greater than the sum of the two numbers following it clockwise. What is the largest number of positive numbers that can be among those written?

A field is a $41\times41$ square of cells, in one of whose cells a tank is camouflaged. A fighter plane fires at one cell with one shot. If there is a hit, the tank crawls to a cell of the field adjacent by a side; if not, it stays in place. After a shot the pilot does not know whether there was a hit. To destroy the tank it must be hit twice. What is the smallest number of shots that suffices to guarantee that the tank is destroyed?

An acute triangle $ABC$ ($AB < AC$) is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the intersection point of its medians and $AH$ an altitude of this triangle. The ray $MH$ meets $\Omega$ at the point $A'$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $A'HB$ is tangent to $AB$.

$N \ge 9$ distinct non-negative numbers less than one are written on the board. It turned out that for any eight distinct numbers on the board there is a ninth one on it, different from them, such that the sum of these nine numbers is an integer. For which $N$ is this possible?

A money changer at a bazaar has many carpets. In exchange for a carpet of size $a\times b$ he agrees to give either a carpet of size $\frac{1}{a}\times\frac{1}{b}$ or two carpets of sizes $c\times b$ and $\frac{a}{c}\times b$ (in each such exchange the client may choose the number $c$ himself). A traveller said that initially he had one carpet whose sides exceeded $1$, and after several such exchanges he had a set of carpets each of which has one side longer than $1$ and the other shorter than $1$. Is he lying? (At the client's request the money changer is ready to regard a carpet of size $a\times b$ as a carpet of size $b\times a$.)

A circle $\omega$ touches the sides of an angle $BAC$ at the points $B$ and $C$. A line $\ell$ meets the segments $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $K$ and $L$ respectively. The circle $\omega$ meets $\ell$ at the points $P$ and $Q$. Points $S$ and $T$ are chosen on the segment $BC$ so that $KS \parallel AC$ and $LT \parallel AB$. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $S$ and $T$ lie on one circle.

Sasha chose a positive integer $N > 1$ and wrote out in a row, in increasing order, all its positive divisors: $d_1 < \dots < d_s$ (so that $d_1 = 1$ and $d_s = N$). Then for each pair of adjacent numbers he computed their greatest common divisor; the sum of the $s-1$ numbers obtained turned out to equal $N-2$. What values could $N$ take?

From a $100\times100$ paper square of cells, $1950$ two-cell rectangles were cut out along the cell boundaries. Prove that from the remaining part one can cut out along the cell boundaries a four-cell figure of the form shown on the sheet (a T-tetromino: three cells in a row and one cell attached to the middle one), possibly rotated. (If such a figure is already among the remaining parts, it is considered to have been cut out.)

Nine (not necessarily distinct) nine-digit numbers are formed from the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$; each digit is used exactly once in each number. What is the largest number of zeros in which the sum of these nine numbers can end?

A square is divided into $n^2 \ge 4$ rectangles by $2(n-1)$ lines, $n-1$ of which are parallel to one side of the square and the other $n-1$ to the other side. Prove that one can choose $2n$ rectangles of the partition such that for any two chosen rectangles one of them can be placed inside the other (possibly after rotating it).

A circle $\omega$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ in which $AB < AC$. The excircle of this triangle touches the side $BC$ at the point $A'$. A point $X$ is chosen on the segment $A'A$ so that the segment $A'X$ does not intersect $\omega$. The tangents drawn from $X$ to $\omega$ meet the segment $BC$ at the points $Y$ and $Z$. Prove that the sum $XY+XZ$ does not depend on the choice of the point $X$.
The sum of positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ equals $3$. Prove the inequality $$\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}+\frac{1}{c^2}+\frac{1}{d^2}\le\frac{1}{a^2b^2c^2d^2}.$$

In a country some pairs of cities are connected by one-way direct flights (between any two cities there is at most one flight). Say that a city $A$ is accessible for a city $B$ if one can fly from $B$ to $A$, possibly with changes. It is known that for any two cities $P$ and $Q$ there is a city $R$ for which both $P$ and $Q$ are accessible. Prove that there is a city for which all cities of the country are accessible. (It is assumed that one can fly from a city to the city itself.)

An isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $BC$ and $AD$ is given. A circle $\omega$ passes through the vertices $B$ and $C$ and meets the side $AB$ and the diagonal $BD$ a second time at the points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. The tangent to the circle $\omega$ at the point $C$ meets the ray $AD$ at the point $Z$. Prove that the points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ lie on one line.

A hundred gnomes whose weights are $1, 2, 3, \dots, 100$ pounds gathered on the left bank of a river. They cannot swim, but on the same bank there is a rowing boat with a carrying capacity of $100$ pounds. Because of the current it is hard to row back, so each gnome has strength enough to row from the right bank to the left at most once (any gnome can row the boat; the rower does not change during one trip). Can all the gnomes cross to the right bank?

Is there an infinite increasing sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ of positive integers such that the sum of any two distinct terms of the sequence is coprime to the sum of any three distinct terms of the sequence?

$n > 3$ distinct positive integers less than $(n-1)! = 1\cdot2\cdot\ldots\cdot(n-1)$ are written on the board. For each pair of these numbers Seryozha divided the larger by the smaller with remainder and wrote the incomplete quotient obtained in his notebook (thus, if he divided $100$ by $7$, he would obtain $100 = 14\cdot7+2$ and would write the number $14$ in the notebook). Prove that among the numbers in the notebook there are two equal ones.

Is it true that for any three distinct positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ there is a quadratic trinomial with integer coefficients and positive leading coefficient taking the values $a^3$, $b^3$ and $c^3$ at some integer points?

A scalene triangle $ABC$ in which $\angle ACB = 60^\circ$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. A point $A'$ is chosen on the bisector of the angle $BAC$ and a point $B'$ on the bisector of the angle $ABC$ such that $AB' \parallel BC$ and $BA' \parallel AC$. The line $A'B'$ meets $\Omega$ at the points $D$ and $E$. Prove that the triangle $CDE$ is isosceles.

Each cell of a $100\times100$ board is coloured either black or white, and all cells adjacent to the boundary of the board are black. It turned out that nowhere on the board is there a monochromatic $2\times2$ square of cells. Prove that there is a $2\times2$ square of cells on the board whose cells are coloured in a chessboard pattern.

Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an infinite increasing sequence of positive integers, and $p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots$ a sequence of prime numbers such that for every positive integer $n$ the number $a_n$ is divisible by $p_n$. It turned out that for all positive integers $n$ and $k$ the equality $a_n - a_k = p_n - p_k$ holds. Prove that all the numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots$ are prime.

A circle $\omega$ touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. A circle $\Omega$ touches the side $AC$ and the extension of the side $AB$ beyond the point $B$, and also touches $\omega$ at a point $L$ lying on the side $BC$. The line $AL$ meets $\omega$ and $\Omega$ a second time at the points $K$ and $M$ respectively. It turned out that $KB \parallel CM$. Prove that the triangle $LCM$ is isosceles.

Let $a_1, \dots, a_{25}$ be non-negative integers, and $k$ the smallest of them. Prove that $$[\sqrt{a_1}]+[\sqrt{a_2}]+\dots+[\sqrt{a_{25}}] \ge \left[\sqrt{a_1+\dots+a_{25}+200k}\right].$$ (As usual, $[x]$ denotes the integer part of the number $x$, that is, the greatest integer not exceeding $x$.)

On an $n\times n$ board of cells several cells were marked so that the lower left ($L$) and upper right ($R$) corners of the board are not marked, and every knight's path from $L$ to $R$ necessarily contains a marked cell. For which $n > 3$ can one assert for certain that there are three consecutive cells along a diagonal among which at least two are marked?

$99$ points dividing a circle into $99$ equal arcs are marked on it. Petya and Vasya play a game, moving alternately. Petya moves first; with his first move he colours any marked point red or blue. Then each player in his move may colour red or blue any uncoloured marked point adjacent to an already coloured one. Vasya wins if, after all points are coloured, there is an equilateral triangle all three vertices of which are coloured, and in the same colour. Can Petya prevent him?
Positive integers $a$ and $b$ are given. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that the number $a^n+1$ is not divisible by $n^b+1$.

In a card game each card is assigned a numerical value from $1$ to $100$, and each card beats a smaller one, with one exception: $1$ beats $100$. A player knows that $100$ cards with distinct values lie face down in front of him. The croupier, who knows the order of these cards, may tell the player, about any pair of cards, which of them beats which. Prove that the croupier can make a hundred such statements so that afterwards the player can determine exactly the value of each card.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the angles $A$ and $C$ are equal. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ there are points $M$ and $N$ respectively such that $MN \parallel AD$ and $MN = 2AD$. Let $K$ be the midpoint of the segment $MN$, and $H$ the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the lines $KH$ and $CD$ are perpendicular.

$5$ points are marked in the plane. Prove that one can choose some of them and move them so that the distance between any two moved points does not change, and as a result a set of $5$ points symmetric with respect to some line remains in the plane.

For what smallest positive integer $n$ do there exist integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ such that the quadratic trinomial $$x^2-2(a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n)^2x+\left(a_1^4+a_2^4+\dots+a_n^4+1\right)$$ has at least one integer root?

A circle $\Omega$ with centre $O$ is circumscribed about an acute triangle $ABC$ in which $AB < BC$; its altitudes meet at the point $H$. On the extension of the segment $BO$ beyond the point $O$ a point $D$ is marked such that $\angle ADC = \angle ABC$. The line through the point $H$ parallel to the line $BO$ meets the smaller arc $AC$ of the circle $\Omega$ at the point $E$. Prove that $BH = DE$.

$10000$ children came to a camp, and each is friends with exactly $11$ other children in the camp (friendship is mutual). Each child wears a T-shirt of one of the seven colours of the rainbow, and any two friends have different colours. The counsellors demanded that some children (at least one) put on T-shirts of other colours (out of the same seven). A survey showed that $100$ children do not intend to change their colour. Prove that some of the remaining children can still change the colours of their T-shirts so that, as before, any two friends have different colours.

In a kindergarten the teacher took $n > 1$ identical cardboard rectangles and handed them out to $n$ children, one rectangle each. Each child cut his rectangle into several identical small squares (the squares of different children could be different). It turned out that the total number of small squares is a prime number. Prove that the original rectangles were squares.

On the side $AC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$ a point $D$ is taken. On the smaller arc $CD$ of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $BCD$ a point $K$ is chosen. The ray $CK$ meets the line parallel to $BC$ and passing through $A$ at the point $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $DT$. Prove that $\angle AKT = \angle CAM$.

Among $16$ coins there are $8$ heavy ones, weighing $11$ g each, and $8$ light ones, weighing $10$ g each, but it is not known which coins have which weight. One of the coins is a jubilee coin. How can one find out in three weighings on a two-pan balance without weights whether the jubilee coin is heavy or light?
Numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, not less than $1$, are given. Prove that $$\frac{a+b+c}{4}\ge\frac{\sqrt{ab-1}}{b+c}+\frac{\sqrt{bc-1}}{c+a}+\frac{\sqrt{ca-1}}{a+b}.$$

$1000$ points are marked on a circle, each coloured in one of $k$ colours. It turned out that among any five pairwise intersecting segments whose endpoints are $10$ distinct marked points, there are at least three segments each of which has endpoints of different colours. For what smallest $k$ is this possible?

Let $n$ be a positive integer. An integer $a > 2$ is called $n$-decomposable if $a^n-2^n$ is divisible by every number of the form $a^d+2^d$, where $d$ is a positive divisor of $n$ different from $n$. Find all composite positive integers $n$ for which there exists an $n$-decomposable number.

$n+1$ distinct segments are marked on a line; one of the points of the line belongs to all these segments. Prove that among the marked segments one can choose distinct segments $I$ and $J$ intersecting in a segment of length at least $\frac{n-1}{n}d$, where $d$ is the length of the segment $I$.

A point $D$ is marked on the side $AB$ of an acute triangle $ABC$, and a point $E$ on the extension of the side $BC$ beyond the point $C$. It turned out that the line through $E$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to the circumcircle of the triangle $ADC$. Prove that one of the tangents drawn from the point $E$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $BCD$ cuts off from the angle $ABE$ a triangle similar to the triangle $ABC$.

Numbers $b > 0$ and $a$ are such that the quadratic trinomial $x^2+ax+b$ has two distinct roots, exactly one of which lies on the segment $[-1;1]$. Prove that exactly one of these roots lies in the interval $(-b;b)$.

Inside a scalene acute triangle $ABC$ in which $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$ a point $T$ is marked such that $\angle ATB = \angle BTC = \angle ATC = 120^\circ$. The medians of the triangle meet at the point $M$. The line $TM$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $ATC$ a second time at the point $K$. Find $TM/MK$.
Positive integers $n > 20$ and $k > 1$ are such that $n$ is divisible by $k^2$. Prove that there exist positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $n = ab+bc+ca$.

A hundred sages were offered the following test. They are brought into a hall one by one (in an order known in advance). In the hall the warden offers each sage a choice of some two distinct numbers from the set $1, 2, 3$. The sage chooses exactly one of them, tells the chosen number to the warden and leaves the hall. Before his choice the sage has the right to learn from the warden which number was chosen by each of the two previous sages (the second sage has the right to learn about the first one). During the test any communication between the sages is forbidden. If at the end the sum of all $100$ numbers chosen by the sages equals $200$, then the sages have failed the test; otherwise they have passed it. Prove that the sages can agree in advance on their actions so as to be guaranteed to pass the test.

Call the main divisors of a composite number $n$ its two largest positive divisors different from $n$. Composite positive integers $a$ and $b$ are such that the main divisors of the number $a$ coincide with the main divisors of the number $b$. Prove that $a = b$.

The bisectors of a triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $I$, and the external bisectors of its angles $B$ and $C$ meet at the point $J$. A circle $\omega_b$ with centre $O_b$ passes through the point $B$ and touches the line $CI$ at the point $I$. A circle $\omega_c$ with centre $O_c$ passes through the point $C$ and touches the line $BI$ at the point $I$. The segments $O_bO_c$ and $IJ$ meet at the point $K$. Find the ratio $IK/KJ$.

$200$ positive integers are written in a row. Of any two neighbouring numbers of the row, the right one is either $9$ times greater than the left one or $2$ times smaller than the left one. Can the sum of all these $200$ numbers equal $24^{2022}$?

There are $18$ children in a class. The parents decided to give the children of this class a cake. For this they first found out from each child the area of the piece he wants to get. After that they ordered a square cake whose area is exactly equal to the sum of the $18$ named numbers. However, on seeing the cake, the children wanted their pieces to be square as well. The parents may cut the cake by cuts parallel to the sides of the cake (the cuts need not begin or end on a side of the cake). For what largest $k$ can the parents be sure to cut out of the ordered cake $k$ square pieces that can be given to $k$ children so that each of them receives what he wants?

An infinite sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots$ is given, no two terms of which are equal. A segment $a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+m-1}$ of this sequence is called a monotone segment of length $m$ if $a_i < a_{i+1} < \dots < a_{i+m-1}$ or $a_i > a_{i+1} > \dots > a_{i+m-1}$. It turned out that for every positive integer $k$ the term $a_k$ is contained in some monotone segment of length $k+1$. Prove that there is a positive integer $N$ such that the sequence $a_N, a_{N+1}, \dots$ is monotone, i.e. $a_N < a_{N+1} < \dots$ or $a_N > a_{N+1} > \dots$.
For what smallest positive integer $a$ do there exist integers $b$ and $c$ such that the quadratic trinomial $ax^2+bx+c$ has two distinct positive roots not exceeding $\frac{1}{1000}$?

There are $998$ cities in a country. Some pairs of cities are connected by two-way flights. According to the law, there must be at most one flight between any pair of cities. Another law requires that for any group of cities there are at most $5k+10$ flights connecting two cities of this group, where $k$ is the number of cities in the group. At present the laws are observed. Prove that the ministry of development can introduce several new flights so that the laws are still observed and the total number of flights in the country becomes $5000$.

A circle $\omega$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ and touches the side $BC$ at the point $K$. The circle $\omega'$ is symmetric to the circle $\omega$ with respect to the point $A$. A point $A_0$ is chosen so that the segments $BA_0$ and $CA_0$ are tangent to $\omega'$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Prove that the line $AM$ bisects the segment $KA_0$.

Two monic quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are given; it is known that the trinomials $f(x)$, $g(x)$ and $f(x)+g(x)$ each have two roots. It turned out that the difference of the roots of the trinomial $f(x)$ equals the difference of the roots of the trinomial $g(x)$. Prove that the difference of the roots of the trinomial $f(x)+g(x)$ is not greater than these differences. (In each difference the smaller root is subtracted from the larger one.)

Initially $250$ letters are written in a row: $125$ letters A and $125$ letters B in some order. Then in one operation one may take any piece of several consecutive letters containing equally many letters A and B, write the letters of this piece in reverse order and at the same time replace all letters A in this piece by letters B and letters B by letters A. (For example, from the string $\mathrm{A\underline{BABBAA}B}$ one operation can produce the string $\mathrm{A\underline{BBAABA}B}$.) Can one write out the initial string and perform several operations so that as a result the board shows the same string with its letters written in reverse order?

Every positive integer greater than $1000$ was coloured either red or blue. It turned out that the product of any two distinct red numbers is blue. Could it happen that no two blue numbers differ by $1$?

A point $X$ lies strictly inside the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$. Denote by $I_B$ and $I_C$ the centres of the excircles of this triangle touching the sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Prove that $XI_B\cdot XI_C > XB\cdot XC$.

If there are several heaps of stones on a table, we say that there are many stones on the table if one can find $50$ heaps and number them from $1$ to $50$ so that the first heap contains at least one stone, the second at least two stones, $\dots$, the fiftieth at least fifty stones. Suppose that initially there are $100$ heaps of $100$ stones each on the table. Find the largest $n \le 10\,000$ such that after removing any $n$ stones from the initial heaps there are still many stones on the table. (When stones are removed, a heap does not split into several heaps.)

Consider all $100$-digit numbers divisible by $19$. Prove that the number of such numbers containing none of the digits $4$, $5$ and $6$ equals the number of such numbers containing none of the digits $1$, $4$ and $7$.

A trapezoid $ABCD$ is given in which $AD \parallel BC$, and the rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at the point $G$. The common external tangents to the circles circumscribed about the triangles $ABC$ and $ACD$ meet at the point $E$. The common external tangents to the circles circumscribed about the triangles $ABD$ and $BCD$ meet at the point $F$. Prove that the points $E$, $F$ and $G$ lie on one line.

Petya has $10\,000$ weights, no two of which have equal weight. He also has a miracle device: if $10$ weights are put into it, it reports the sum of the weights of some two of them (it is not known which ones). Prove that Petya can use the miracle device so that after some time he can point to one of the weights and name its weight exactly. (Another number of weights cannot be put into the miracle device.)

Petya and Vasya know only the positive integers not exceeding $10^9-4000$. Petya considers good the numbers representable in the form $abc+ab+ac+bc$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers not less than $100$. Vasya considers good the numbers representable in the form $xyz-x-y-z$, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are positive integers greater than $100$. Which of them has more good numbers?
A positive integer has exactly $50$ divisors. Could it happen that no difference of two distinct divisors of it is divisible by $100$?
problems.proposer: Methodological commission, after a problem of A. Chironov

problems.problem: Two boys were each given a sack of potatoes, each sack containing $150$ tubers. The boys take turns moving potatoes: in his move each boy moves a non-zero number of tubers from his own sack into the other's sack. They must observe the condition of new opportunity: in each move a boy must move more tubers than he had in his sack before any of his previous moves (if there were such moves). Thus, with his first move a boy may move any non-zero number, and with his fifth move a boy may move $200$ tubers if before his first, second, third and fourth moves the numbers of tubers in his sack were less than $200$. What is the largest total number of moves the boys can make?

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ in which $\angle A+\angle D = 90^\circ$ is given. Its diagonals meet at the point $E$. A line $\ell$ meets the segments $AB$, $CD$, $AE$ and $ED$ at the points $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and $T$ respectively. It is known that $AZ = CE$ and $BE = DT$. Prove that the length of the segment $XY$ equals the diameter of the circumcircle of the triangle $ETZ$.

A block is a $10\times10$ square of cells. On New Year's night snow suddenly fell for the first time, and since then exactly $10$ cm of snow has fallen on every cell every night; snow fell only at night. Every morning the yard-keeper chooses one row (a row or a column) and shovels all the snow from it onto one of the neighbouring rows (from each cell onto the cell adjacent to it by a side). For example, he may choose the seventh column and shovel all the snow from each of its cells into the cell to its left. Snow may not be shovelled outside the block. On the evening of the hundredth day of the year an inspector will come to the town and find the cell with the highest snowdrift. The yard-keeper's goal is to make this height minimal. What height of snowdrift will the inspector find?

The altitudes of an acute triangle $ABC$ in which $AB < AC$ meet at the point $H$, and $O$ is the centre of its circumcircle $\Omega$. The segment $OH$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $BHC$ at a point $X$ different from $O$ and $H$. The circumcircle of the triangle $AOX$ meets the smaller arc $AB$ of the circle $\Omega$ at the point $Y$. Prove that the line $XY$ bisects the segment $BC$.

$8$ distinct quadratic trinomials are written on the board; no two of them add up to the zero polynomial. It turned out that if one chooses any two trinomials $g_1(x)$, $g_2(x)$ from the board, the remaining $6$ trinomials can be labelled $g_3(x), g_4(x), \dots, g_8(x)$ so that all four polynomials $g_1(x)+g_2(x)$, $g_3(x)+g_4(x)$, $g_5(x)+g_6(x)$ and $g_7(x)+g_8(x)$ have a common root. Must all the trinomials on the board have a common root?

$1000$ children, no two of the same height, stood in a line. Call a pair of distinct children $(a, b)$ good if between them there is no child whose height is greater than the height of one of $a$ and $b$ but less than the height of the other. What is the largest number of good pairs that could be formed? (The pairs $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$ are considered the same pair.)

Several segments parallel to the sides of a rectangular sheet of paper were drawn on it. These segments divided the sheet into several rectangles inside which there are no drawn lines. Petya wants to draw one diagonal in each of the rectangles of the partition, dividing it into two triangles, and colour each triangle either black or white.
