Is it true that he can always do this so that no two triangles of the same colour have a common segment of boundary?

The diagonals of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at the point $E$. The points of tangency of the circumcircles of the triangles $ABE$ and $CDE$ with their common external tangents lie on a circle $\omega$. The points of tangency of the circumcircles of the triangles $ADE$ and $BCE$ with their common external tangents lie on a circle $\gamma$. Prove that the centres of the circles $\omega$ and $\gamma$ coincide.
Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists an even positive integer $a$ such that the number $(a-1)(a^2-1)\ldots(a^n-1)$ is a perfect square.

A chess king was placed on a cell of an $8\times8$ board and made $64$ moves so that it visited all cells and returned to the initial cell. At every moment the distance from the centre of the cell in which the king was to the centre of the whole board was computed. Call a move pleasant if as a result of the move this distance became smaller than it was before the move. Find the largest possible number of pleasant moves. (In one move a chess king moves to a cell adjacent by a side or by a corner.)

Let $P_1(x)$ and $P_2(x)$ be monic quadratic trinomials, and let the points $A_1$ and $A_2$ be the vertices of the parabolas $y = P_1(x)$ and $y = P_2(x)$ respectively. Denote by $m(g(x))$ the smallest value of a function $g(x)$. It is known that the differences $m(P_1(P_2(x)))-m(P_1(x))$ and $m(P_2(P_1(x)))-m(P_2(x))$ turned out to be equal positive numbers. Find the angle between the line $A_1A_2$ and the line containing the axis $Ox$.

Petya chose $100$ pairwise distinct positive numbers less than $1$ and arranged them around a circle. Then he performs operations with them. In one operation one may take three consecutive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ (in exactly this order) and replace the number $b$ by $a-b+c$. For what largest $k$ could Petya choose the initial numbers and perform several operations so that afterwards there are $k$ integers among the numbers?

The numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, 60$ are written in a row (in exactly this order). Igor and Ruslan take turns placing the signs $+$, $-$ and $\times$ between them, Igor beginning; in one move each places one sign. When a sign has been placed between every two neighbouring numbers, the value of the resulting expression is computed. If it is divisible by $3$, Igor is declared the winner, otherwise Ruslan. Which of the players can win regardless of the opponent's actions?

Points $D_1$, $D_2$, $E_1$, $E_2$, $F_1$, $F_2$ are chosen on the perimeter of a triangle $ABC$ so that, going round the perimeter, the points occur in the order $A$, $F_1$, $F_2$, $B$, $D_1$, $D_2$, $C$, $E_1$, $E_2$. It turned out that $AD_1 = AD_2 = BE_1 = BE_2 = CF_1 = CF_2$. Prove that the perimeters of the triangles formed by the triples of lines $AD_1$, $BE_1$, $CF_1$ and $AD_2$, $BE_2$, $CF_2$ are equal.

Initially there are $75$ sweets on a plate. Petya and Vasya take turns taking any positive integer number of sweets from the plate until no sweets remain on the plate. Petya begins. For what smallest $k$ can Petya play so as to guarantee that at the end of the game the numbers of sweets the boys have differ by at most $k$? (The boys do not eat sweets during the game.)

Call a positive integer $n$ strange if there exist pairwise distinct positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $e$, greater than $1$, such that $n = a^{a^a} = b^{b^c} = d^{e^e}$. Is the number of strange numbers finite or infinite? (Recall that $x^{y^z}$ denotes the number obtained by raising the number $x$ to the power $y^z$.)

A scalene triangle $ABC$ in which $\angle A = 60^\circ$ is given. On the side $BC$ points $X$ and $Y$ are marked such that $2BX = AB$ and $2CY = AC$. Prove that there is a circle passing through the points $X$ and $Y$ which is tangent to the incircle and to one of the excircles of the triangle $ABC$.

Several participants from $n$ regions came to an olympiad; some of them are friends (friendship is always mutual). It turned out that for any seating of several (at least three) participants at a round table in which any two neighbours are friends, the participants from each region at the table make up at most half of the total number of children at the table. Prove that the participants can be accommodated in $n$ rooms so that any two friends are in different rooms.

Katya has $2n$ reels with tape ($n$ is a positive integer). Initially $1^2, 2^2, \dots, (2n)^2$ decimetres of tape are wound on the reels respectively. Every hour Katya chooses a positive integer $i$ and cuts $i$ decimetres of tape off every reel on which at least $i$ decimetres of tape remain. After some time all the reels that initially had an odd number of decimetres of tape turned out to be empty. Prove that at this moment the length of the tape remaining on each of the other reels is less than $4n$ decimetres.

The point $O$ is the circumcentre of an acute scalene triangle $ABC$. From the point $A$ perpendiculars $AP$ and $AQ$ were dropped to the extensions of the segments $BO$ and $CO$ beyond the point $O$. The circle with centre $T$ passing through the points $P$ and $Q$ is tangent to the segment $BC$. Prove that $TO \parallel BC$.

Let $n$ be an odd positive integer. An $n\times n$ table is given. Call the distance between two cells of the table the smallest number of steps needed to get from one cell to the other, moving each time to a cell adjacent by a side (thus the distance between cells adjacent by a side equals $1$). $R$ cells of the table are coloured red and the other $B$ cells blue. It is known that no line joining the centres of a red and a blue cell is parallel to either of the diagonals of the table. Moreover, the distance between any red and any blue cell is not equal to $n$. Prove that $\sqrt{R}+\sqrt{B} \le n$.
A triangle with distinct positive integer side lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$ is given. Prove that at least one of the numbers $ab+1$, $bc+1$ and $ca+1$ is not a perfect square.
